neighbours.label: The hyphenated word 'bed-wetting', particularly its continuation piece.
fire: A parent borrowed a booklet about bed-wetting from the school library.
The family discussed bed-wetting calmly during the appointment.
Our survey included a question about bed-wetting in childhood.
The support group shared practical experiences of bed-wetting without blaming the children.
An article on bed-wetting appeared in the monthly parenting magazine.
The teacher asked whether bed-wetting was making overnight trips difficult.
In the glossary, bed-wetting appears between two longer entries.
The proofreader checked the hyphen in the expression bed-wetting.
quiet: From the school library, a parent borrowed a booklet about nighttime accidents.
At the appointment, the family calmly discussed difficulties with bladder control at night.
A childhood survey asked about waking up with wet sheets.
Without blaming the children, the support group discussed staying dry through the night.
The parenting magazine published an article about nighttime incontinence.
For overnight trips, the teacher asked about problems with wet bedding.
Between two longer glossary entries, the phrase nighttime accidents appears.
A proofreader checked the spacing in the phrase wet bedding.

notes: The strongest lexical probe peaked on etting in bed-wetting. Repeated compound names gave little separation, and the card includes many unrelated split words. This is a deliberately narrow compound hypothesis, tested against the same nighttime-accident meaning without that spelling.
